scores.accuracy_concern: Cummings 2018 is a post hoc analysis of FREEDOM and Lyu 2020 is observational; 'several spinal fractures at once' needs the absolute rates (about 1 versus about 7 per 100 person-years) to avoid alarm; the illustrative timeline must not read as a real case.
scores.sharpen: Give the absolute fracture rates after stopping instead of 'several spinal fractures at once' and add what to do if the due date has already passed (contact the GP now and ask about a switch plan).

scores.accuracy_concern: NICE TA279 still recommends vertebroplasty or balloon kyphoplasty in a narrow group with severe ongoing pain after a recent unhealed fracture, and the sham-trial evidence is for vertebroplasty, not kyphoplasty; the positive VAPOUR result must be stated plainly.
scores.sharpen: Separate vertebroplasty from balloon kyphoplasty and state NICE's narrow indication so the position reads as consistent with UK guidance.

scores.accuracy_concern: Deardorff 2022 time to benefit comes from postmenopausal women with osteoporosis in trials, not frail people near the end of life (whose higher baseline risk could shorten it); STOPPFrail criterion wording must be checked; the denosumab caveat should state that rebound fractures appear from several months after a missed dose.
scores.sharpen: Put the verified 12-month time to benefit in the first line and add one sentence that stopping the tablet is a review of the drug's likely benefit while pain relief, falls care and comfort continue.

scores.accuracy_concern: VITAL analysed participants with lower baseline vitamin D and found no clear benefit there either (few were severely deficient), so 'says little about deficient people' must be framed as limited evidence, not untested; Chapuy combined calcium with vitamin D; the D-Health hazard ratio needs checking.
scores.sharpen: Acknowledge VITAL's lower-vitamin D subgroup so the argument is about limited evidence in deficiency, and say Chapuy tested calcium and vitamin D together.

scores.accuracy_concern: The proposed caption 'The number went up. The fractures did not go down.' is a mirrored aphorism (banned shape); vertebral fractures were not significantly different (163 versus 136), and the SABRE meta-regression citations are unverified.
scores.sharpen: Replace the mirrored caption with a literal one (spine density rose by about a third; fractures away from the spine were about three times as common) and keep the line that approved drugs' density gains do track fracture reduction across trials.

scores.accuracy_concern: The 41.1% figure is from dialysis-dependent women aged 65 and over in an observational study; the FDA boxed warning covers advanced CKD more broadly and UK product wording differs, so the two should not be merged.
scores.sharpen: Keep the 41% figure tied to dialysis-dependent women and give the calcium monitoring timing from the product information instead of a placeholder.

scores.accuracy_concern: Proportions with prodromal pain and bilateral fractures must come from the Shane 2014 full text; Black 2020 benefit-harm figures need their denominator and time period; thigh pain has common other causes.
scores.sharpen: Add the next step when plain X-rays are normal but pain continues (MRI or isotope bone scan) and keep the Black 2020 benefit-harm comparison with its denominator.

scores.accuracy_concern: The claim that swallowing assessments and medicine lists are 'rarely read side by side' is unsupported; the SmPC contraindications are oesophageal abnormalities that delay emptying and inability to stay upright for 30 minutes, not dysphagia as such; alendronate oral solution and effervescent forms exist.
scores.sharpen: Drop the unsupported 'rarely' and add one line that liquid or effervescent alendronate exists but still needs the full glass and 30 minutes upright.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'Never felt by the person' overstates: morphometric fractures can cause pain and height loss without being diagnosed; FREEDOM figures and any proportion of vertebral fractures that come to clinical attention need a source.
scores.sharpen: Replace 'never felt' with 'not diagnosed at the time' and show all three bar pairs per 100 women over 3 years.

scores.accuracy_concern: Evidence is from a 2014 Cochrane review with variable trial durations, so '11 fewer per 1,000' needs its timeframe; any current NICE NG249 statement on hip protectors is unverified.
scores.sharpen: Add a question a family can ask the care home (has a hip protector been offered that fits and can be removed quickly at the toilet?) to make it usable.

scores.accuracy_concern: NOGG continuation criteria include age 70 or over and a hip T-score of -2.5 or lower as well as the listed fractures and glucocorticoid dose; FLEX showed fewer clinical vertebral fractures only, and the HORIZON extension morphometric vertebral fractures only; the reassessment interval needs verification.
scores.sharpen: Use NOGG's exact continuation criteria and reassessment interval in the flow diagram and replace the placeholders before drafting.

scores.accuracy_concern: Martyn-St James 2008 found some femoral neck benefit in sensitivity analyses and studied postmenopausal women, not men; cohort studies link walking with fewer hip fractures, so the post must stay with bone density and not imply walking does nothing for fracture risk.
scores.sharpen: Keep the claim to bone density, say walking is still linked with fewer hip fractures in cohort studies, and show two named strength or impact exercises with how often to do them.

scores.accuracy_concern: The 42.4% acute-phase figure includes background symptoms (11.7% with placebo); UK guidance makes an oral bisphosphonate first line, so the form is not a free choice; zoledronic acid needs a kidney function check; denosumab rebound should be stated with absolute rates.
scores.sharpen: Add that UK guidance usually starts with the tablet, so the useful question is: if the tablet routine will not work for me, can we use the injection or the drip instead?

scores.accuracy_concern: Absorption figures come from a pharmacokinetic study in volunteers and do not show a loss of fracture protection; the 'more than 85% with breakfast' figure needs checking against Gertz 1995.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the plain instruction and give the absorption figure second, saying it came from a volunteer absorption study and not from fracture outcomes.

scores.accuracy_concern: VERO compared two drugs over 24 months rather than a sequence; both trials were in postmenopausal women only; romosozumab is contraindicated after heart attack or stroke; UK access criteria (NICE TA791, teriparatide) need checking.
scores.sharpen: Define very high risk in one plain line and add the romosozumab contraindication after heart attack or stroke, which applies to many older people.

scores.accuracy_concern: FRAXplus (from 2023) offers optional adjustments for fracture recency and number of falls, so 'FRAX does not ask' must specify the standard calculator; the NOGG list of situations where FRAX underestimates risk must be quoted exactly.
scores.sharpen: Name FRAXplus and the NOGG adjustments so the post teaches how to correct for recency, number of fractures and falls rather than implying the tool has no answer.

scores.accuracy_concern: The COMPASS fracture hazard ratio and interval must come from the full text; follow-up was 3 years in a cardiovascular trial population, so 'did not show a clear difference' must not become 'no effect'.
scores.sharpen: Report the COMPASS fracture result with its range from the full text and name the 3-year follow-up and cardiovascular population as limits.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'Vague caution tends to mean less movement, weaker muscles and more falls' is a causal chain not shown in Brooke-Wavell 2022 and should be labelled as judgement; lifting advice must match the consensus wording on spinal flexion.
scores.sharpen: Mark the point about vague caution as judgement, keep the four instructions verbatim from the consensus, and schedule it well apart from C04-03, which uses the same source.

scores.accuracy_concern: Trigger thresholds (height loss of 4 cm, glucocorticoids for 3 months or more) must match NOGG 2022 wording; falls as a reassessment trigger is less explicit in NOGG and needs a source.
scores.sharpen: Make each trigger match NOGG wording exactly and add that a review can be requested at any GP appointment rather than waiting for a recall.

scores.accuracy_concern: Persistence range (about 18% to 75% at 12 months) must be checked against Fatoye 2019; the opening claim that 'far fewer' services can report 12-month persistence needs FLS-DB figures or should go; persistence and adherence are different measures; Imaz 2010 is observational.
scores.sharpen: Open with the verified persistence range as a plain natural frequency and drop the unsupported comparison of what services count unless FLS-DB completeness figures are opened.

scores.accuracy_concern: Shahinian 2005 is observational, so fracture excess is 'linked with' ADT; NICE NG131 and NG101 wording (consider versus offer assessment) must be checked, and those NICE pages may not open.
scores.sharpen: Offer a men-first opening for the prostate version and verify the NICE recommendations through a published summary or NOGG 2022, which can be opened.

scores.accuracy_concern: The position 'base the decision on the hip when spine and hip disagree' is too broad: a genuinely lower spine T-score (for example with glucocorticoids) is valid and the WHO diagnosis uses the lowest valid site; Liu 1997 is an old cohort.
scores.sharpen: Narrow the position to 'when the spine looks better than the hip' and state that a genuinely lower spine result still counts.

scores.accuracy_concern: A New Zealand trial selected by T-score; UK treatment decisions use FRAX thresholds and zoledronate is not licensed by T-score category, so the post could be read as advising treatment outside guidance; secondary findings (deaths, cancer) must not be presented as benefits.
scores.sharpen: State that UK decisions use FRAX thresholds rather than the osteopenia label and give the absolute figures per 100 women over 6 years alongside the number needed to treat.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'Some people stop their bone medicine because of calcium tablets' needs a source or should go; the WHI kidney stone finding was for calcium plus vitamin D; NOGG target (700 to 1,200 mg) and food calcium values must be verified.
scores.sharpen: Drop the unsourced claim about stopping bone medicine and give the NOGG daily target with three common foods' verified calcium content.

scores.accuracy_concern: About 4 in 10 had symptoms after a first infusion but about 1 in 10 did with placebo, so the drug-attributable figure is about 3 in 10; second and third infusion rates need verification.
scores.sharpen: Give the placebo comparison in the first line and add the practical prompt about drinking well beforehand and paracetamol afterwards from the product information.

scores.accuracy_concern: The 82% figure (Siris 2004) comes from peripheral (heel, wrist, finger) densitometry in US women over one year and should not be presented as a hip DXA finding; 'most fractures occur in osteopenia' partly reflects how many people fall in that band.
scores.sharpen: Add what to do with the answer (ask whether your FRAX result is above or below the treatment threshold for your age) and name the scan method behind the 82% figure.

scores.accuracy_concern: Constant relative effect across ages is an assumption the HIP trial's over-80 result partly contradicts; competing mortality reduces absolute benefit; illustrative icon arrays risk being read as trial data; the Boonen analyses are unverified.
scores.sharpen: Put the HIP trial over-80 null result in the main text, not a footnote, and replace invented icon arrays with published FRAX age-band probabilities.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'Daily or weekly doses are the safer way' is an inference: Sanders 2010 shows harm from 500,000 IU yearly, not proof that daily dosing is safer; Bischoff-Ferrari 2016 compared doses (no placebo) with falls as a secondary outcome.
scores.sharpen: Aim it at prescribers and replace 'safer' with 'avoid the yearly single-dose schedule that increased falls and fractures in a trial'.

scores.accuracy_concern: Montori 2011 was a small trial (100 women) and figures need checking; better understanding is not the same as better decisions; the NICE bisphosphonate decision aid's title and status are unverified.
scores.sharpen: Use real published figures in the icon array rather than an illustrative one, and state in the caption that the decision aid did not change how many started treatment.

scores.accuracy_concern: SACN, PHE and NICE PH56 are official web documents that may not open from this environment, leaving only search extracts; UK wording is 'take' for people rarely outdoors or in care homes but 'consider' for people with dark skin, and this should be reproduced exactly.
scores.sharpen: Anchor the advice in a source that can be opened (NICE PH56 PDF or a published SACN summary) and end with one concrete check: is vitamin D on the medicine chart, and is it being given?

scores.accuracy_concern: Haasum 2012 figures (25% versus 7%, OR 0.34) need full-text verification and come from cross-sectional Swedish data of the early 2000s; ZEST was underpowered for fractures; no dementia-fracture meta-analysis has yet been identified.
scores.sharpen: Verify or update the undertreatment data and lead with the more distinctive point that a yearly drip or 6-monthly injection removes the tablet-routine barrier for people with dementia.

allocation_reason: All 31 candidates clear the 36-point bar and at least 18 are strong, distinct and supported by trials, Cochrane reviews or product information, while avoiding the earlier treatment-gap angles, so the category merits the top of the range even after merging the overlapping clusters (tablet routine: 06/09/13; vitamin D: 05/20/21; trial numbers: 27/29/30; exercise: 03/18).
balance_note: Of the top 14 by score, 6 are for practitioners (24, 29, 16, 09, 30, 14), 5 for both (17, 04, 20, 26, 03) and only 3 for the public (07, 06, 13), and 06 and 13 overlap on the tablet routine. To strengthen the public and carer share, swap 13 or 30 for 12 (Ask this: what would change a no-treatment decision) or 22 (cancer hormone treatment, which also reaches men). Men are otherwise barely represented because most of the trial evidence is in postmenopausal women. Reading the evidence dominates the top group (17, 20, 29, 30, 24, 03), so series spread needs attention; the only Care that works candidate (27) is weak.
